## 

For this Research Project I

will using SQL for data investigation and cleaning, and Python for statistical analysis and investigation.

to investigate this central question:

How does energy performance vary across NYC buildings, and what data quality issues could affect the reliability of energy-efficiency assessments?

Import Data

```{R}
library(readr)

building_data <- read_csv(
  "/Users/beepbop/Downloads/NYC_Building_Energy_and_Water_Data_Disclosure_for_Local_Law_84_2023_to_Present_(Data_for_Calendar_Year_2022-Present)_20261012.csv"
)
```

```{R}
problems(building_data)
```

Parsing issue is because numbers within data sets include commas, which causes inconsistencies

```{R}
names(building_data)[250:251]
```

Fix issue and re import the data

```{R}
building_data <- read_csv(
  "/Users/beepbop/Downloads/NYC_Building_Energy_and_Water_Data_Disclosure_for_Local_Law_84_2023_to_Present_(Data_for_Calendar_Year_2022-Present)_20261012.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    `Number of Active Energy Meters - Total` = col_character(),
    `Number of Active Energy Meters - Used to Compute Metrics` = col_character(),
    .default = col_guess()
  )
)
 # parse_number() coverst va;uses into numbers
building_data$`Number of Active Energy Meters - Total` <-
  parse_number(building_data$`Number of Active Energy Meters - Total`) 

building_data$`Number of Active Energy Meters - Used to Compute Metrics` <-
  parse_number(building_data$`Number of Active Energy Meters - Used to Compute Metrics`)

problems(building_data)
```

After fixing the parsing issues our NYC building energy data set now contains 103,259 rows and 265 columns.

Need to determine how many repeated property-year records differ only in reporting dates, and how many contain differences in energy or building information?


```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

con <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(),
  dbname = "nyc_building_energy.sqlite"
)
dbIsValid(con)
```

Add Data to SQLite

```{r}
dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "buildings",
  building_data,
  overwrite = TRUE
)
# Creates table "buildings" and copies R data frame into it
dbListTables(con)
```

Verify all records were transferred correctly

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_records
  FROM buildings;
")
```

Check the number of records by year, to understand distribution

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS total_buildings
  FROM buildings
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
```

Investigate Duplicate Property Records

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    "Property ID",
    COUNT(*) AS record_count
  FROM buildings
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year", "Property ID"
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year", record_count DESC
  LIMIT 10;
')
```

Count repeated property-year combinations

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS repeated_properties
  FROM (
    SELECT
      "Calendar Year",
      "Property ID"
    FROM buildings
    GROUP BY "Calendar Year", "Property ID"
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
  ) AS duplicates
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
```

This presents a data quality issue where multiple submissions for the same property and reporting year could distort energy performance calculations if we count them separately.

Before removing anything, we need to determine whether the repeated records contain different energy measurements.

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT 
    "Calendar Year",
    SUM(record_count -1) AS extra_records 
  FROM(
    SELECT 
    "Calendar Year",
    "Property ID",
    COUNT(*) AS record_count
  FROM buildings
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year", "Property ID"
  HAVING COUNT(*) >1
  ) AS duplicates
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
    
#SUM(record_count -1) Calcualtes how many additional rows exist beyond the first record
```

Check whether the repeated record have different energy values

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    "Property ID",
    COUNT(*) AS record_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)") AS distinct_eui_values 
  FROM buildings
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year", "Property ID"
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
  ORDER BY distinct_eui_values DESC, record_count DESC
  LIMIT 10;
')

 #If distinct_eui_values greater than 1 the property has conflicting energy measurnments across records
```

Some properties have different energy consumption values reported for the same calendar year.

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Property ID",
    "Calendar Year",
    "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)",
    "Report Generation Date",
    "Report Submission Date"
  FROM buildings
  WHERE "Property ID" = 5834470
    AND "Calendar Year" = 2023
  ORDER BY "Report Submission Date";
')
```

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN "Report Submission Date" IS NULL
          OR TRIM("Report Submission Date") = ""
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS missing_submission_dates
  FROM buildings;
')
```

Check missing submission dates by year

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN "Report Submission Date" IS NULL
          OR TRIM("Report Submission Date") = ""
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS missing_dates
  FROM buildings
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')

```

All the repeated property-year groups occur in years where submission dates are available. We can therefore use submission dates to identify the latest report for each repeated property-year combination.

Convert submission dates into a sortable format

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Report Submission Date" AS original_date,
    substr("Report Submission Date", 7, 4) || "-" ||
    substr("Report Submission Date", 1, 2) || "-" ||
    substr("Report Submission Date", 4, 2) || " " ||
    printf("%02d",
      (CAST(substr("Report Submission Date", 12, 2) AS INTEGER) % 12) +
      CASE
        WHEN substr("Report Submission Date", -2) = "PM"
        THEN 12
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) ||
    substr("Report Submission Date", 14, 6) AS formatted_timestamp
  FROM buildings
  WHERE "Property ID" = 5834470
    AND "Calendar Year" = 2023
  ORDER BY formatted_timestamp;
')
```

Identify the latest submission for every property-year combination

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Property ID",
    "Calendar Year",
    "Report Submission Date",
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY "Property ID", "Calendar Year"
      ORDER BY
        substr("Report Submission Date", 7, 4) || "-" ||
        substr("Report Submission Date", 1, 2) || "-" ||
        substr("Report Submission Date", 4, 2) || " " ||
        printf("%02d",
          (CAST(substr("Report Submission Date", 12, 2) AS INTEGER) % 12) +
          CASE
            WHEN substr("Report Submission Date", -2) = "PM"
            THEN 12
            ELSE 0
          END
        ) ||
        substr("Report Submission Date", 14, 6) DESC
    ) AS submission_rank
  FROM buildings
  WHERE "Property ID" = 5834470
    AND "Calendar Year" = 2023
  ORDER BY submission_rank;
')
# used ROW_NUMBER() to rank records within each property-year combination

```

Create cleaned SQL table where only the latest submission is kept

```{r}
dbExecute(con, '
  DROP TABLE IF EXISTS buildings_clean;
')

dbExecute(con, '
  CREATE TABLE buildings_clean AS
  WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
      *,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY "Property ID", "Calendar Year"
        ORDER BY
          substr("Report Submission Date", 7, 4) || "-" ||
          substr("Report Submission Date", 1, 2) || "-" ||
          substr("Report Submission Date", 4, 2) || " " ||
          printf("%02d",
            (CAST(substr("Report Submission Date", 12, 2) AS INTEGER) % 12) +
            CASE
              WHEN substr("Report Submission Date", -2) = "PM"
              THEN 12
              ELSE 0
            END
          ) ||
          substr("Report Submission Date", 14, 6) DESC
      ) AS submission_rank
    FROM buildings
  )
  SELECT *
  FROM ranked
  WHERE submission_rank = 1;
')
```

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS cleaned_records
  FROM buildings_clean;
')
```

The cleaned data set now contains 102,484 which is 775 records less then the original data set.

Verify that no property-year duplicate remains

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT 
    "Property ID",
    "Calendar Year",
     COUNT(*) AS record_count
  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Property ID", "Calendar Year"
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
')

```

No duplicate property-year combinations remain

Check for missing values

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT 
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,
    COUNT("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)") AS records_with_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
  ')
```

every record seems to have a non-NULL site EUI value

Check for EUI sites that could be blank or containing empty strings such as "NA"

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN TRIM("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)") = ""
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS blank_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
```

Site EUI column has no SQL NULL values and no blank strings

Check whether all values in Site EUI are valid numbers

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT DISTINCT
    "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS site_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" GLOB "*[^0-9.]*"
  LIMIT 20;
')
# *[^0-9.]* looks for values containing at least one character that isisnt a digit (0-9) or a decimal point 
```

Negative EUI values do not make sense because EUI measures energy consumed per square foot. Not Available will be treated as missing data.

Before deciding how to handle them we should make sure these values aren't tied to one year or condition.

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,

    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" = "Not Available"
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS unavailable_eui,

    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) < 0
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS negative_eui

  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
```

From this it can be seen that there is a large portion of unavailable EUI records for each year. However, 2024 contains the largest amount of unavailable EUI records.

Calculate Valid Site SUI records

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    COUNT(*) AS valid_eui_records
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != "Not Available"
    AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
```

I will exclude these values from the energy performance analysis because unavailable measurements cannot be used to calculate energy intensity, and negative Site EUI values are not physically meaningful for ordinary building energy consumption. Including these records could produce misleading results, particularly when calculating average energy intensity.

Now I will begin to analyze how reporting building energy intensity compares across years?

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    ROUND(AVG(CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL)), 2) AS avg_site_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != "Not Available"
    AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY "Calendar Year";
')
```

An average of 15,018.12 in 2023 is unusually high. This might be caused by extreme outliers that are pulling averages upward.

Look for outliers in the Site EUI values

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year",
    "Property ID",
    "Primary Property Type",
    "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS site_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != "Not Available"
    AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0
  ORDER BY CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) DESC
  LIMIT 10;
')
```

The data set contains reported Site EUI values in the millions of kBtu/ft²

This is very high for energy use per square foot. This could be due to reporting errors, incorrect units, or another issue in the underlying data.

I will first check if these extreme values are associated with specific property types.

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Primary Property Type - Self Selected" AS property_type,
    COUNT(*) AS total_records
  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Primary Property Type - Self Selected"
  ORDER BY total_records DESC
  LIMIT 15;
')
```

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Property ID",
    "Property Name",
    "Primary Property Type - Self Selected" AS property_type,
    "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS site_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Property ID" = 4038924
    AND "Calendar Year" = 2023;
')
```

The most extreme EUI is associated with Multifamily Housing. A typical multifamily building should not have a EUI measured in the millions. This could be a reporting error or data quality issue. This does explain however why the averages were so high. It can be seen a small number of extreme values can drastically increase the mean.

I will compare the mean and median

```{r}
eui_values <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
      "Calendar Year" AS year,
      "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS site_eui
    FROM buildings_clean
    WHERE "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != "Not Available"
      AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0;
      ')
# AND CST() takes site EUI values and converst it into a number that can contain decimals.
eui_values$site_eui <- as.numeric(eui_values$site_eui)
aggregate(site_eui ~ year, data = eui_values, FUN = median)
# aggregate(site_eui ~ year) groupes site EUI values by calander year
```

The median values are much more reasonable. The mean values differed so much because a relatively small number of extreme high Site EUI values pull the mean upward. In order to decide what to do with the extreme values I will first try an understand their distribution.

Calculate the 90th and 99th percentile

```{r}
percentiles <- aggregate(
  site_eui ~ year,
  data = eui_values,
  FUN = function(x) quantile(x, probs = c(0.50, 0.90, 0.99))
)
print(percentiles)
```

visualize

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
percentiles <- data.frame(
  year = percentiles$year,
  percentiles$site_eui
)

percentiles_long <- pivot_longer(
  percentiles,
  cols = -year,
  names_to = "percentile",
  values_to = "site_eui"
)

ggplot(percentiles_long,
       aes(x = year, y = site_eui, color = percentile)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "NYC Building Site EUI Percentiles (2022–2024)",
    x = "Calendar Year",
    y = "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)",
    color = "Percentile"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

From this we can see that the extreme Site EUI values are concentrated in the upper tail of the distribution. I will keep the original values but use the median for initial year to year comparisons.

Find the amount of records that exceed a Site EUI of 1,000 per year

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year" AS year,
    COUNT(*) AS extreme_records
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) > 1000
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY year;
')

```

How common are these extreme values

```{r}
extreme_eui <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year" AS year,
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) > 1000
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS extreme_records
  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Calendar Year"
  ORDER BY year;
')

extreme_eui$percentage <- round(
  extreme_eui$extreme_records / extreme_eui$total_records * 100,
  2
)

print(extreme_eui)
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(extreme_eui,
       aes(x = factor(year), y = percentage)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Extreme Site EUI Values in NYC Buildings",
    subtitle = "Percentage of records with Site EUI above 1,000 kBtu/ft²",
    x = "Calendar Year",
    y = "Percentage of Records"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.7),
    breaks = seq(0, 0.7, 0.1),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Records reporting Site EUI above 1,000 kBtu/ft² represented less than 1% of observations in each year. The highest proportion occurred in 2023 (0.55%), compared with 0.22% in 2022 and 0.41% in 2024. Although these observations were uncommon, their unusually high values substantially influenced the annual mean Site EUI. These records were retained in the cleaned dataset for further investigation, while median values were used to describe typical energy performance.

Do extreme values belong to particular building types

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Primary Property Type - Self Selected" AS property_type,
    COUNT(*) AS extreme_records
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) > 1000
  GROUP BY "Primary Property Type - Self Selected"
  ORDER BY extreme_records DESC
  LIMIT 10;
')
```

Multifamily Housing accounts for approximately 53.4% of all 410 extreme records. However, Multifamily Housing also accounts for most records in our dataset (68,103). That means having the highest number of extreme records doesn't necessarily mean multifamily buildings are the most likely to report extreme EUI.

Calculate the percentage within each property type

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Primary Property Type - Self Selected" AS property_type,
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,

    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) > 1000
        THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS extreme_records,

    ROUND(
      100.0 * SUM(
        CASE
          WHEN CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) > 1000
          THEN 1
          ELSE 0
        END
      ) / COUNT(*),
      2
    ) AS percentage_extreme

  FROM buildings_clean
  GROUP BY "Primary Property Type - Self Selected"
  ORDER BY extreme_records DESC
  LIMIT 10;
')
```

Laboratory type properties have the highest proportion of extreme values. Laboratories may use more energy than residential buildings because of specialized equipment and ventilation requirements.

Calculate median Site EUI by property type and year

```{r}
property_eui <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Calendar Year" AS year,
    "Primary Property Type - Self Selected" AS property_type,
    "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS site_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != \'Not Available\'
    AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0;
')

property_eui$site_eui <- as.numeric(property_eui$site_eui)

median_by_type <- aggregate(
  site_eui ~ year + property_type,
  data = property_eui,
  FUN = median
)

head(median_by_type, 10)
```

Pick out the median Site EUI by property type and year for thr 5 most common property types

```{r}
major_types <- c(
  "Multifamily Housing",
  "Office",
  "K-12 School",
  "Hotel",
  "College/University"
)

major_eui <- median_by_type[
  median_by_type$property_type %in% major_types,
]

print(major_eui)
```

Visualize

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(major_eui,
       aes(x = year, y = site_eui, color = property_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Site EUI by NYC Property Type",
    subtitle = "2022–2024",
    x = "Calendar Year",
    y = "Median Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)",
    color = "Property Type"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Now lets look at how many observations contribute to each median, because a median based on a small. number of observations is less representative then one based on many more.

Count observations by property type and year

```{r}
library(dplyr)

property_counts <- property_eui %>%
  group_by(year, property_type) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(property_counts, 10)

median_by_type <- aggregate(
  site_eui ~ year + property_type,
  data = property_eui,
  FUN = median
)

median_by_type <- left_join(
  median_by_type,
  property_counts,
  by = c("year", "property_type")
)

median_by_type <- median_by_type %>%
  select(year, property_type, site_eui, n)
head(median_by_type, 10)

```

```{r}
major_eui <- median_by_type %>%
  filter(property_type %in% c(
    "Multifamily Housing",
    "Office",
    "K-12 School",
    "Hotel",
    "College/University"
  ))

print(major_eui)
```

Visualizations

```{r}

ggplot(major_eui,
       aes(x = year,
```

Identify buildings that reported in all three years

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS buildings_with_valid_eui
  FROM (
    SELECT
      "Property ID"
    FROM buildings_clean
    WHERE "Property ID" IS NOT NULL
      AND "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != \'Not Available\'
      AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0
    GROUP BY "Property ID"
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT "Calendar Year") = 3
  );
')
```

```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

matched_eui <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Property ID" AS property_id,
    "Calendar Year" AS year,
    "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS site_eui
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Property ID" IS NOT NULL
    AND "Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" != \'Not Available\'
    AND CAST("Site EUI (kBtu/ft²)" AS REAL) >= 0;
')

matched_eui$site_eui <- as.numeric(matched_eui$site_eui)

matched_eui <- matched_eui %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = site_eui
  ) %>%
  drop_na(`2022`, `2023`, `2024`)

nrow(matched_eui)
head(matched_eui, 10)
```

Calculate the percentage change in Site EUI for each building between 2022 and 2024.

```{r}
matched_eui <- matched_eui %>%
  mutate(
    eui_change = `2024` - `2022`,
    percent_change = (`2024` - `2022`) /
      na_if(`2022`, 0) * 100
  )

# na_if prevents division by zero
head(matched_eui, 10)
```

Summarize the changes

```{r}
matched_eui %>%
  summarise(
    total_buildings = n(),
    decreased = sum(eui_change < 0),
    increased = sum(eui_change > 0),
    unchanged = sum(eui_change == 0),
    median_change = median(eui_change),
    median_percent_change = median(percent_change, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Most of the buildings reported lower Site EUI in 2024 then in 2022.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

change_summary <- matched_eui %>%
  summarise(
    Decreased = sum(eui_change < 0),
    Increased = sum(eui_change > 0),
    Unchanged = sum(eui_change == 0)
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "change",
    values_to = "buildings"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = buildings / sum(buildings) * 100
  )

ggplot(change_summary,
       aes(x = change, y = percentage)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%")),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Changes in Site EUI Among Matched NYC Buildings",
    subtitle = "21,708 buildings with valid data in 2022, 2023, and 2024",
    x = "Change from 2022 to 2024",
    y = "Percentage of Buildings"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 75)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Compare the matched building changes by property type to help answer which NYC building types experienced the greatest changes in Site EUI between 2022 and 2024, when comparing the same buildings?

```{r}
property_types <- dbGetQuery(con, '
  SELECT
    "Property ID" AS property_id,
    "Primary Property Type - Self Selected" AS property_type
  FROM buildings_clean
  WHERE "Calendar Year" = 2022;
')

matched_eui <- matched_eui %>%
  select(-starts_with("property_type")) %>%
  left_join(property_types, by = "property_id")
head(matched_eui)
nrow(matched_eui)
```

Compare changes by property type

```{r}
change_by_type <- matched_eui %>%
  group_by(property_type) %>%
  summarise(
    buildings = n(),
    median_percent_change = median(percent_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    percent_decreased = mean(eui_change < 0) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(buildings >= 100) %>%
  arrange(median_percent_change)

change_by_type
```

```{r}
ggplot(change_by_type,
       aes(x = reorder(property_type, median_percent_change),
           y = median_percent_change)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Site EUI Change by Building Type",
    subtitle = "Same NYC buildings, 2022–2024 (n ≥ 100 per type)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median Change in Site EUI (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Investigate K-12 schools

```{r}
school_eui <- matched_eui %>%
  filter(property_type == "K-12 School") %>%
  summarise(
    median_2022 = median(`2022`),
    median_2023 = median(`2023`),
    median_2024 = median(`2024`)
  )

school_eui
```

The median fell sharply between 2022 and 2023 and remained mainly unchanged between 2023 and 2024.

```{r}
matched_eui %>%
  filter(property_type == "K-12 School") %>%
  summarise(
    change_2022_2023 = median(
      (`2023` - `2022`) / na_if(`2022`, 0) * 100,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    change_2023_2024 = median(
      (`2024` - `2023`) / na_if(`2023`, 0) * 100,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
```

I will compare the changes across other building types to see if this pattern is unique to school buildings.

```{r}
yearly_changes <- matched_eui %>%
  group_by(property_type) %>%
  summarise(
    buildings = n(),
    change_22_23 = median(
      (`2023` - `2022`) / na_if(`2022`, 0) * 100,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    change_23_24 = median(
      (`2024` - `2023`) / na_if(`2023`, 0) * 100,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(buildings >= 100) %>%
  arrange(change_22_23)

yearly_changes
```

It seem a big decline in Site EUI between 2022 and 2023 followed by small change between 2023 and 2024 is seen across multiple building types.

The widespread decrease in Site EUI between 2022 and 2023 may partly reflect changes in building occupancy and operations following the COVID-19 pandemic. However, differences in weather conditions, energy use, and reporting practices may also have contributed. Further analysis would be needed to determine what drove these changes.
